title: Meet the tools before using them
why: A tool error is easier to fix when you know which program has the job.
outcome: Identify your editor, terminal, Node, npm, and Git.

steps.title: Start with what you know
steps.question: What replaces the C toolchain?
explanation: In C, you edit source files, compile them, then run the program. Here you will edit TypeScript, check its types, produce JavaScript, then run that JavaScript with Node.
Your editor changes files. Your terminal runs commands. Node runs JavaScript outside a browser. npm installs local tools and runs named scripts. Git records changes.

steps.title: Check before installing
steps.question: Which tools are already available?
explanation: Run the version checks below one at a time. A printed version means the program was found. “command not found” means the shell cannot find it.

If Node or npm is missing on macOS, open the official Node download page (https://nodejs.org/en/download), choose the LTS installer for your Mac, install it, reopen the terminal, and rerun the checks. Node includes npm. If Git is missing, run git --version and follow macOS’s developer-tools prompt.

The practice configuration uses TypeScript 5.9.3 and Vitest 4.1.11. Their declared Node ranges include Node 24 and 26; this course’s rehearsal uses Node 26.10.0. Keep the version you checked in your notes.

steps.title: Know the fields
steps.question: Why are these dependencies development tools?
explanation: private prevents accidental npm publishing. type: module selects import/export modules. scripts names commands. devDependencies lists tools used to build and test this project.
TypeScript provides tsc. Vitest runs tests. @types/node describes Node APIs for the checker; those descriptions are not runtime code. package-lock.json records the resolved install for repeatability.

steps.title: Build and run separately
steps.question: Why does the caller import a .js filename?
explanation: Your source is .ts. In this NodeNext setup, TypeScript produces .js files in dist/. Node executes those JavaScript files. A relative import names the emitted .js file so Node can find it.
export makes a function available to another module. import names what the caller needs. A module is a file with imports or exports; you do not create C-style header files for this example.
